sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Gefjun** (*gefjon*) ​— Fertility, ‌Agriculture · Giver ‌— is ​the ploughing goddess ​of the ​Norse tradition: the ​Æsir-born woman who ​accepted King ‌Gylfi's wager of ​a plough-land ​— as much ‌as four ​oxen could turn ‌up in ​a day and ‌a night ​— and answered ​it by ​tearing the island ​of Zealand ​out of Sweden ‌and setting it ​in the ‌sea.[^1]

The name ​is transparent ‌Old Norse: *Gefjun* ​derives from ‌*gefa* 'to give' ​— the ‌giver.[^2] Snorri numbers ​her fourth ​among the ásynjur, ‌with the ‌single startling office ‌that 'she ​is a maiden, ​and those who ‌die maidens ​serve her'; the ​Poetic Edda ‌gives her one ​speaking part, ​in *Lokasenna*, where ‌she intervenes ​against Loki and ‌is answered ​with a taunt ​about a ​fair lad and ​a bright ‌necklace.[^1][^3]

Her one ‌great narrative opens ​the Prose ‌Edda itself: four ​sons begotten ​on a giant ‌of Jötunheimr, ‌shape-changed into oxen, ‌a ploughshare ‌driven deep enough ​to tear ‌the land loose, ​and a ​kingdom's worth of ​soil dragged ‌west into the ​sea — leaving ​Lake Mälaren ​behind in Sweden ‌as the ​mould the island ​was cast ​from.[^1] PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Gefjun** — ‌already plain ​ASCII in normalized ‌Old Norse, ​which places it ‌in Tier ‌2 — and ​claims no domain ​for it: ​the plain-ASCII gefjun.com ​is held ‌outside the collection ‌and watched ​for release.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1 (the ploughing of Zealand) and the catalogue of the ásynjur, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Gefjun, gefa.
Lokasenna 20–22 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old Norse ‌as **Gefjun** ​(nominative; genitive *Gefjunar*). ​It derives ​transparently from ​the verb *gefa* ​'to give' ‌— the same ​word as ​English *give* and ‌German *geben* ​— hence 'the ‌giver, the ​giving one'.[^1] The ‌name's closest ​divine relative ​is **Gefn**, listed ​in Gylfaginning ​among the bynames ​of [[freyja|Freyja]] ‌and standing on ​the same ‌root; the sources ​keep Gefjun ‌and Gefn distinct, ​though scholars ‌have long ​suspected a deeper ‌connection.[^2]

The ​ASCII working form ​*gefjon* is ‌a modern respelling ‌of the ‌ending as *-jon*; ​the manuscripts ​write only *-jun*. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Gefjun** ​is itself plain ‌ASCII — ​normalized Old Norse ​puts no ‌diacritic and no ​distinctive letter ‌in this name ​— so ​the mechanical rule ​places it ​in Tier ‌2, an honest ‌report about ​orthography rather than ‌a judgment ​on the goddess.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ‌**g** → ‌**G** — Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**e** → ‌**e** — Same
​- **f** ​→ **f** — ​Same
- ‌**j** → **j** ​— Same
​- **o** → ​**u** — ‌Normalized Old Norse ​*-jun*: the ​manuscripts write ​u, not o
‌- **n** ​→ **n** — ‌Same

The ​project holds no ‌domain for ​this name. The ‌plain-ASCII **gefjun.com** ‌is registered to ​a third ​party outside ​the PuniCodex collection ​and is ‌watched for release; ‌this temple ​claims none.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Gefjun, gefa.
Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Gefjun, gefa, Gefn.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gefa, Gefjun.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/ˈɡev.jun/** — ​Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Ge-** — ​Voiced velar ‌stop [ɡ], as ​in English ​*give*, and short ‌front [e], ​as in ‌*bed*; the stressed ​first syllable, ‌as in ​every Old Norse ​word
- ​**-f-** — ​The labiodental fricative, ​voiced toward ‌[v] between ​the vowel and ‌the glide, ​as in ‌*gefa* itself
- ​**-jun** — ‌Palatal glide [j], ​short close ‌back [u], ​and dental [n]; ​the manuscripts ‌write this ‌ending *-jun*, never ‌*-jon*

For ​the modern ​speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: ​'GEV-yoon' — ​the g hard, ‌the e ​short, the ​second syllable like ‌'yoon' with ​a light v-glide ‌before it.

​Kindred and ​historical forms of ​the name:

​- **Old ‌Norse** — Gefjun, ‌the ploughing ​goddess; from ‌*gefa* 'to give'
​- **The ​root verb** ‌— *gefa*, 'to ‌give', the ‌same word ‌as English *give*
​- **Freyja's ‌byname** — Gefn, ​'the giver', ​from the ​same root[^2]
- ‌**Modern Icelandic** ​— Gefjun, ​unchanged; older English ​books write ‌the Latinized ​Gefion

Gefjun is ​Tier 2 ​because the ‌restoration preserves nothing ​the ASCII ‌alphabet cannot ​carry: no diacritic, ‌no distinctive ​letter, no vowel ‌length. The ‌name's information ​survives transit whole ​— the ​only loss ​in the common ‌English spelling ‌'Gefion' is ​historical accuracy.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Gefjun, Gefn.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌medieval Icelandic ​manuscripts in ​the Latin ​alphabet as ​**Gefjun** — ​Old Norse ‌(North Germanic), ​attested 13th–14th ​c. CE ‌in the ​Codex Regius ‌(for Lokasenna) ​and the ‌codices of ​the Prose ​Edda and ​Heimskringla, recording ​material centuries ​older.[^1] No ‌runic attestation ​of the ‌theonym survives; ​the manuscript ‌form is ​the primary ‌witness.

The ​scholarly rendering ‌proceeds step ​by step:

​- The ‌name derives ‌from *gefa* ‌'to give', ​with the ​agentive force ‌'the giving ​one'.
- ​Normalized Old ‌Norse orthography ​writes the ​ending *-jun*: ‌glide j ​plus short ‌u. The ​manuscripts know ​no *-jon*; ​the English ​spelling 'Gefion' ‌is a ‌Latinized modernism.
​- No ‌diacritic and ​no distinctive ​letter occurs ‌anywhere in ‌the name ‌— the ‌restoration Gefjun ​is plain ‌ASCII, which ​is why ​the mechanical ​tier rule ‌classifies it ​Tier 2.[^2]
​- Because ​the name ‌is pure ​ASCII, the ​matching domain ​gefjun.com was ‌registered long ​ago in ‌the ordinary ​way; it ‌is held ​by a ‌third party ‌outside the ​PuniCodex collection ​and watched ​for release, ​and this ‌temple claims ‌no domain ​at all.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Gefjun.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Gefjun** ​is catalogued ‌under Fertility, ‌Agriculture — ​and ​the sources ​earn both ​terms with ​a single ‌instrument: ​the plough.[^1]

​### Fertility

‌Her myth ​is ‌a creation ​myth of ‌the most ​fertile kind: ​land ​itself brought ​forth by ​a goddess ‌and ​her giant-born ‌sons. Scholars ​have long ‌placed ​her among ‌the fertility ​figures of ‌the North, ​though ​the sources ‌give her ‌no cult ‌and ​the classification ​rests on ‌the myth's ​shape rather ​than ‌on ritual ​evidence.[^2]

### ​Agriculture

She ‌is ​the only ‌figure in ​the Norse ​corpus ​who works ​with a ‌plough: the ‌plough-land — ​a ‌day and ​a night's ​ploughing by ‌four ‌oxen — ‌is both ‌the wager's ​unit and ‌the ​myth's measure, ​and creation ​happens by ‌furrow, ​not by ​thunder.

### ​The Giver

‌The ​name's root, ​*gefa* 'to ​give', frames ‌the whole ​story: ‌Gylfi's gift ​of a ‌plough-land is ​answered ‌by a ‌gift beyond ​measuring, and ​the byname ​Gefn ​carries the ‌same root ‌into [[freyja|Freyja]]'s ​house.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Gefjun, Gefn.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Gefjun ‌is the ​iconography ​of her ​single ​great deed ​— ‌the corpus ​gives ​her no ‌temple ​regalia, but ‌the ​ploughing fixed ‌a ​set of ​attributes ​no retelling ​can ​omit:[^1]

- ‌**The plough** ​— ‌Creation by ​furrow: ‌land made ​by ‌turning earth, ​the ‌oldest technology ​of ​order doing ‌the ‌work of ‌a ​god
- ​**The ‌four oxen** ​— ​Her sons ‌by ​a giant ​of ‌Jötunheimr, shape-changed ​into ‌draught-beasts: giant ​strength ​yoked to ​a ​goddess's purpose; ‌Bragi ‌counts eight ​eyes ‌and four ​heads
​- **The ‌plough-land** ‌— The ‌wager's ‌unit, a ​day ‌and a ​night's ​ploughing, stretched ​within ‌its own ​terms until ​it ​holds an ‌island
​- **The ​answering ​coasts** — ‌Zealand's ​headlands and ‌the ​bays of ‌Lake ​Mälaren, the ‌two ‌halves of ​one ​tear: the ​myth's ​own map, ‌and ‌its standing ​evidence[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 5, trans. Lee M. Hollander (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1964).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Gefjun's mythology is a ​single great deed with a small ‌orbit of notices around it: the ‌ploughing of Zealand, told twice — as ​myth in the Edda, as dynastic ​history in Heimskringla — and witnessed ​by one of the oldest skaldic stanzas ​we have.[^1]

### The Plough-Land of ​King Gylfi (Gylfaginning 1)

Gylfi, king ‌of the lands now called Sweden, gave ​a wandering beggar-woman, as reward for ​her entertainment, one plough-land in his ‌realm — as much as four oxen ​could plough up in a day ‌and a night. The woman was ​of the family of the Æsir, and ‌her name was Gefjun. She took ​four oxen out of Jötunheimr — ​her own sons by a certain giant ​— and set them before the ​plough; the share went so deep ​and hard that it tore the land ‌loose, and the oxen drew it ​out into the sea and westward until ‌it stopped in a sound. There ​she set the land and named ‌it Selund, Zealand. Where the land had ​been, the water filled in: the ‌lake now called Lögrinn, Mälaren, whose ​bays correspond to Zealand's headlands.[^1]

### The ‌Völva and the Founding of Lejre ​(Ynglinga saga 5)

Heimskringla's version frames ​the making as history: Gefjun was a ‌*spákona*, a seeress, and [[odinn|Óðinn]] sent ‌her north across the sound to ‌look for land. Gylfi met her and ​gave the plough-land; she went to ​Jötunheimr, bore four sons to a ‌giant, changed them into oxen's likeness, and ​drew the land out westward opposite ​Óðinsvé, Odense. The saga then adds ‌what the Edda omits: Gefjun settled on ​her new-made land and married Skjöldr, ​a son of Óðinn, and their ‌seat was Hleiðra — Lejre, beside Roskilde, ​the royal seat of Denmark. The ‌maker of the island stood at ​the root of its kings: Skjöldr is ​the eponym of the Skjöldungar, the ​Scyldings.[^2]

### Eight Eyes and Four ​Heads (Bragi inn gamli)

Both Snorri and ‌the saga close with the same ‌four lines attributed to Bragi inn ​gamli Boddason, the ninth-century skald — the ‌oldest datable witness to the myth. ​In the stanza's kennings, Gefjun gladly ​drew from Gylfi 'the wave-trove's free-hold' until ‌smoke rose from the running sweat-beasts, ‌and the oxen bore 'eight forehead-moons ‌and four heads' as they carried off ‌Denmark's increase. The story was already ​fixed, with fixed imagery, centuries before ‌Snorri wrote.[^2]

### Fourth Among the Ásynjur ​(Gylfaginning)

In Snorri's catalogue of the ​ásynjur, Gefjun stands fourth, after [[frigg|Frigg]], ​Sága, and Eir, with one startling office: ‌'she is a maiden, and those ​who die maidens serve her.' The catalogue's ​maiden and the myth's giant-consort are ​never reconciled; Skáldskaparmál keeps her in ‌the þulur of the ásynjur and licenses ​her name as a base-word in ​kennings for women.[^1]

### The Necklace ​and the Fair Lad (Lokasenna 20–22)

Her ‌single speaking part in the Poetic ​Edda comes at Ægir's feast: as ‌[[loki|Loki]] works his way down the bench ​of goddesses, Gefjun intervenes — why ‌do you Æsir bandy bitter words ​in the hall? Óðinn rebukes her at ‌once: she is mad to rouse ‌Loki, for Loki knows the fates ​of all as well as Óðinn himself. ​Loki's answer is the only scandal ​the corpus attaches to her: a ​fair youth gave her a bright necklace, ‌a *sigli*, and she wound her ‌legs about him. Nothing answers the ​taunt; nothing repeats it.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1 and the catalogue of the ásynjur; Skáldskaparmál þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 5 (quoting Bragi inn gamli), trans. Hollander (1964).
Lokasenna 20–22 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Gefjun's ​nearest relative ‌lives inside ‌the pantheon ​itself. Gylfaginning ​names **Gefn** ​— 'the ​giver' — ​among the ‌bynames of ​[[freyja|Freyja]], and ​both names ‌stand on ​the same ‌root, *gefa*; ​Simek treats ‌Gefjun and ​Gefn as ​possibly once-connected ​figures whom ​the surviving ​sources keep ‌distinct.[^1]

Beyond ​the North, ‌scholars have ​long set ‌her story ​among the ‌land-measure foundation ​legends of ‌the ancient ​world — ​tales in ‌which a ‌people explains ‌how its ​territory was ​won by ‌stretching a ​definition, Dido's ​ox-hide at ‌Carthage being ​the classical ​case. The ‌Norse ​variant stretches ‌not a ​hide but ​a day's ​ploughing, and ​the unit ‌it stretches ‌is agricultural: ​the plough-land.[^1] ‌Her other ​life is ​dynastic. Through ‌Skjöldr she ‌belongs to ‌the origin-complex ‌of the ​Danish kings ‌— the ​same stratum ​that produced ​*Beowulf*'s Scyld ‌Scefing, the ​sheaf-child who ​founds the ​Scylding line ‌in the ​poem's prologue, ​and Saxo's ​Skioldus. The ‌handbooks read ​the marriage ‌of Gefjun ​and Skjöldr ‌as the ​point where ‌myth and ‌royal genealogy ​were deliberately ​joined: a ​plough-goddess at ​the root ‌of a ‌farming aristocracy's ​line.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Gefjun, Gefn.

Beowulf, prologue (Scyld Scefing and the Scylding line), ed. and trans. R. M. Liuzza, 2nd ed. (Peterborough, ON: Broadview, 2013); Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gefjun.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Gefjun's ​afterlife is ‌monumental and ‌national. ​The Gefion ​Fountain on ​Copenhagen's harbourfront ​— ​Anders Bundgaard's ‌great bronze ​group, ​unveiled in ‌1908 as ​the Carlsberg ‌Foundation's ​gift to ‌the city ​— ​shows her ​exactly where ​the ​myth leaves ‌her: driving ​the four ‌oxen ​as they ‌strain toward ​the ‌sea. It ​is among ‌the ​largest monuments ​in Copenhagen ‌and the ‌standard ‌image of ​the goddess ​worldwide, ‌and the ​story itself ​remains Denmark's ‌foundation ​tale, the ​way Danish ‌children ​learn why ‌Zealand lies ​apart ​in the ​sea.[^1]

Her ​name has ‌even ‌left the ​planet: the ‌main-belt ​asteroid 1272 ​Gefion, discovered ‌in 1931, ‌gives ‌its name ‌to the ​Gefion ‌family of ​asteroids. In ​the ​North the ‌name never ​became a ​common ​given name, ‌and modern ​Heathenry ​keeps her ​chiefly as ‌the ​goddess of ‌the land ​itself — ‌but ​in Denmark ‌she needs ‌no ​introduction, and ​her fountain ​is where ​Copenhagen ‌meets its ‌own creation ​story.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gefjun.
Davidson, H. R. Ellis, Gods and Myths of Northern Europe (Harmondsworth: Penguin, 1964), on the fertility deities and the ploughing myth.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Gefjun ​is a ‌textual goddess ‌whose evidence ​is a ​landscape. Her ​attestations are ​literary — ​the Codex ‌Regius *Lokasenna*, ​Snorri's Gylfaginning, ​and the ‌Ynglinga saga ​of Heimskringla ‌— and ​no cult ‌site, votive ​deposit, or ​runic inscription ​names her; ​the place-name ​claims sometimes ‌advanced on ​her behalf ‌are insecure.[^1] ​What the ‌myth itself ​offers as ‌evidence is ​the map: ‌Zealand's headlands ​and the ​bays of ‌Lake Mälaren, ‌explained by ‌the story ​as the ​two halves ‌of a ​single tear.

​Her one ‌fixed point ​on the ​ground is ‌Hleiðra — ​Lejre, near ‌Roskilde — ​where the ​saga seats ​her marriage ​to Skjöldr. ‌Excavations there ‌since the ​1980s have ‌uncovered successive ​great-hall complexes ​of the ‌Iron Age ‌and Viking ‌Age, confirming ‌Lejre's real ​antiquity as ‌a royal ​power centre ​behind the ​Skjöldung legends, ‌though nothing ​found names ​the goddess ​herself.[^2] The ‌oldest datable ​witness to ​the myth ​is not ‌a stone ​but a ‌stanza: Bragi's ​ninth-century verse, ‌quoted by ​both Snorri ‌and the ‌saga. Her ​most famous ​monument is ​modern: Bundgaard's ​Gefion Fountain, ‌unveiled in ‌Copenhagen in ​1908.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gefjun.
Christensen, Tom, Lejre – Syn og Sagn (Roskilde: Roskilde Museum, 1991), on the Lejre hall excavations.

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic ​Edda gives ‌Gefjun exactly ‌one speaking ​part, and ​it costs ​her. In ​*Lokasenna* 20–22, ​at Ægir's ‌feast, she ​intervenes as ​Loki works ‌down the ​bench of ‌goddesses: why, ​she asks, ‌do you ​Æsir bandy ​bitter words ​in the ​hall? Óðinn's ​rebuke is ‌immediate — ​she is ‌mad, he ​says, to ‌rouse Loki, ​for Loki ‌knows the ​fates of ‌all as ​well as ​Óðinn himself. ‌Then Loki ‌turns on ‌her with ​the corpus's ​only scandal ‌against her ​name: a ​fair youth ‌gave her ​a bright ​necklace, a ‌*sigli*, and she ​wound her ‌legs about ​him.[^1]

The ​exchange is ​instructive for ​what it ‌assumes. Gefjun ‌sits in ​the full ‌company of ​the goddesses, ​ranked among ‌those Loki ‌thinks worth ‌insulting; Óðinn's ‌answer treats ​her as ‌a peer ​who should ​have known ​better; and ‌the necklace-taunt ​pairs her, ​deliberately or ​not, with ‌the necklace-stories ​of [[freyja|Freyja]]. ​Beyond Lokasenna ​the mythological ‌poems are ​silent about ‌her — ​the ploughing ‌of Zealand, ​the story ‌that defines ‌her, belongs ​to the ​prose tradition ​and the ​skaldic stanza ‌it quotes, ‌not to ​Eddic verse.[^2]

sources.citation: Lokasenna 20–22 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gefjun.

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The ​Prose Edda ‌is Gefjun's ‌great witness, ​and it ​puts her ​first: Gylfaginning ​1 opens ​the whole ‌work with ​the ploughing ​of Zealand, ‌before Gylfi ​ever sets ‌out for ​Ásgarðr. Snorri's ‌telling has ​the chronicle's ​plainness — ​the beggar-woman, ​the reward ​of a ‌plough-land, the ​four oxen ‌out of ​Jötunheimr who ‌were her ​own sons ‌by a ​giant, the ‌share that ​tore the ​land loose, ‌the drawing ‌of it ‌westward into ​a sound, ​the naming ‌of Selund, ​and the ​water that ‌filled the ​wound to ​become Lögrinn, ‌Mälaren, with ​bays answering ‌Zealand's headlands. ​The chapter ​closes by ​quoting Bragi's ​stanza as ‌proof.[^1]

Later, ‌in the ​catalogue of ‌the ásynjur, ​Snorri numbers ​her fourth ‌— after ‌[[frigg|Frigg]], Sága, ‌and Eir ‌— with ​the office ‌that 'she ​is a ​maiden, and ​those who ‌die maidens ​serve her', ​a sentence ​the Zealand ‌myth never ​explains. Skáldskaparmál ​preserves her ​in the ‌þulur of ​the ásynjur ‌and licenses ​her name ‌as a ​base-word in ‌kennings for ‌women: a ​skald could ​call any ​woman a ​Gefjun of ‌her treasures, ‌and the ​verse-tradition did.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1 and the catalogue of the ásynjur, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the ásynjur and woman-kennings, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains no ‌invocation of ​Gefjun: ​no runestone ​asks her ​favour, ​no amulet ‌bears her ​name, and ​no ‌inscription links ​a dedicant ‌to ​her cult ‌— a ​silence she ​shares ​with most ​of the ​ásynjur ‌and one ​that marks ‌her as ​a ‌literary-mythological figure ​rather than ‌an ​epigraphic one.[^1]

‌Had the ​name been ​carved ‌in the ‌Viking Age, ‌it ​would have ​stood in ‌the Younger ​Futhark ​as roughly ‌ᚴᛁᚠᛁᚢᚾ (k-i-f-i-u-n): ​the ​k-rune writes ‌g, the ​single i-rune ‌covers ​both the ​vowel e ​and ​the glide ‌j, and ‌the ᚢ ​carries ‌the short ​u. The ​rendering ‌is a ‌normalized reconstruction, ‌not an ‌attested ​carving; the ‌primary witness ​remains ​the manuscript ​spelling of ‌the Eddas. ​The ​name's raw ​material is ‌transparent ​vocabulary — ​*gefa* 'to ​give' is ‌one ​of the ‌commonest verbs ​in ‌the language ​— so ‌the theonym ‌needs ​no exotic ​explanation: the ​giver, ​walking out ‌of the ‌word-pool into ​mythology.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gefjun.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. gefa.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Gefjun's medieval ‌afterlife is ​dynastic. Heimskringla's ​Ynglinga saga ​(ch. 5) ​retells the ​ploughing as ‌the ​prehistory of ​the Danish ‌crown: Gefjun ​is a ‌*spákona*, a ​seeress, sent ‌north by ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] to ​look ​for land; ​Gylfi gives ​the plough-land; ‌the four ​giant-born sons ‌become oxen; ​and the ‌land ​is drawn ‌out westward ​opposite Óðinsvé, ‌Odense. The ​saga then ​makes the ‌myth a ‌foundation: Gefjun ‌settles ​on her ​island, marries ‌Skjöldr, a ​son of ​Óðinn, and ‌keeps her ​seat at ​Hleiðra — ‌Lejre, ​the royal ‌estate beside ​Roskilde from ​which the ​Skjöldung line ​of Danish ‌kings was ‌held to ​descend.[^1]

‌The euhemerizing ​frame matters: ​where Gylfaginning ‌tells a ‌myth about ‌a goddess, ‌Ynglinga saga ​tells history ‌about ​a remarkable ​woman in ​Óðinn's train, ‌and the ​two versions ​together show ​how a ‌single ​story could ​serve both ​the theological ‌and the ​genealogical bookshelf. ‌The þulur ​in Skáldskaparmál ‌keep her ​catalogued ‌among the ‌ásynjur beside ​[[frigg|Frigg]] and ​[[fulla|Fulla]], a ​goddess of ​one great ‌deed preserved ‌with bureaucratic ​fidelity.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 5, trans. Lee M. Hollander (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1964).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the ásynjur, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Gefjun ​is ‌the patron ‌of ​the ​answer ​that ​exceeds the ​wager. ‌Gylfi ​sets ​the ‌terms — ​four ‌oxen, ​a ‌day and ​a ​night ​— ​and ​keeps his ‌word; ​she ‌keeps ​it too, ‌and ​ruins ‌him ​within ‌the terms.[^1] ​The ​myth ‌is ‌about ‌measure outwitted ​by ​measure: ‌the ​smallest unit ​of ‌farmland, ​a ​plough-land, ‌stretched until ​it ‌holds ​an ​island ​and a ​royal ‌house.

‌What ​she gives ‌is ​not ​only ‌the ‌land but ‌the ‌lesson ​the ‌name ​already carries: ​the ​giver ‌decides ​the scale ​of ​the ‌gift. ​Every ​telling of ​her ‌is ​a ‌reminder that ​the ‌terms ​you ‌set ‌will be ​met ​— ​by ​someone ‌cleverer at ‌keeping ​them.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 1, trans. Faulkes (1987).
